title: Facts are hares, truth is a tortoise
lede: Millions of studies are published every year, and many disagree. Here is how to tell strong evidence from weak.

stats.label: average time for one systematic review

ladder.name: Anecdote
ladder.note: One person's story. Cannot separate cause from chance.

ladder.name: Single study
ladder.note: A lead worth testing. Findings often fail to hold up.

ladder.name: Observational study
ladder.note: Shows association, but other factors may explain it.

ladder.name: Randomised trial
ladder.note: Tests cause directly, but one trial can still mislead.

ladder.name: Systematic review
ladder.note: Pools and appraises all relevant studies. The strongest test of a claim.

voteCounting.heading: Why counting studies misleads
voteCounting.body: Four papers say wine is unhealthy and five say it is not. Counting suggests the five win. But if the five studied only five people each and the four studied 5,000, the count hides what matters: sample size and quality.
voteCounting.fix: A systematic review weighs each study instead of counting it.

policies.heading: What could governments do?
policies.intro: Ideas for discussion, based on the problems in the article. Each one has a trade-off.

items.title: Label the strength of health claims
items.tradeoff: Hard to enforce; labels can oversimplify.

items.title: Set standards for AI summaries of research
Teach evidence literacy
items.fixes: Readers cannot tell strong from weak.
items.tradeoff: Slow, and results are hard to measure.

timeline.text: A study says babies should sleep face down.
A hugely popular childcare guide changes its advice to match. Sudden infant deaths rise.
Reviews of earlier studies lead governments to advise sleeping on the back. The earlier advice may have cost up to 50,000 lives.

voteDemo.heading: Try it: count vs weigh
voteDemo.intro: Change the numbers. Counting studies and weighing them can give different winners.
voteDemo.weighLine: Weighing participants: {winner} has more evidence ({a} vs {b} people).

cases.title: Paracetamol in pregnancy
cases.text: Systematic reviews found no clear link with autism or ADHD in children.

cases.title: Management fads
cases.text: Reviews suggest many standard practices, such as performance appraisals, lack strong evidence that they help.

viral: Reviews take about three years on average and are costly. AI summaries can hallucinate. Meanwhile a tentative single study travels fast, so myths and fads keep flying.
sources: Based on 'Facts Are Hares, But Truth Is A Tortoise' (Mindfield, TOI), drawing on Helen Pearson's Beyond Belief.
